demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping

Memory.value: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power
Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
My life has been destroyed by the trauma

issues.explanation: For trauma type 'unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one', the body-focused appraisals 'I can no longer trust my own body' and 'I feel ashamed of what happened to my body' are hard to reconcile clinically unless the patient also directly experienced major bodily violation/injury, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile.

The memory items imply vivid sensory reliving of the traumatic event ('hear things ... heard during the frightening event') and fragmented visual snapshots, which can occur in PTSD, but here they are not well matched to the selected appraisals: the profile centers on bodily shame/unreliability rather than grief/death-related meanings of the event.

'Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study' is not impossible, but in this profile it appears weakly integrated: there are no trigger or threat items tying work contexts to the trauma, and the formulation does not include trigger/threat pathways. The coping profile otherwise concerns sleep delay and undereating, so work avoidance feels insufficiently anchored.

issues.item: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: For trauma involving the unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one, body-focused shame is clinically hard to reconcile unless there was also direct bodily violation, injury, or assault. The rest of the profile centers grief-related loss, meaning, and intrusive memory phenomena, so this item appears inconsistent with the trauma type and with the other selected items.

vignette:
Leilani, a 46-year-old forensic analyst, sat across from me, her exhaustion palpable despite her meticulous appearance. Her marriage, she explained, was under immense strain, and her work performance, once a source of pride, had plummeted, prompting her to finally seek help. Her life had irrevocably changed eighteen months prior, on the day her beloved 16-year-old son, Kael, was killed instantly in a car accident. She remembered receiving the call, the sudden, jarring ring of her phone, and then the guttural cry from her husband. In the immediate aftermath, Leilani found herself caught in a horrifying tableau, the image of the crumpled vehicle and the flashing lights of the emergency services seared into her mind.

Now, memories of that day return to Leilani not as a flowing narrative, but as a series of disjointed, vivid "Snapshot Memories." She sees the mangled metal, the paramedics' grave faces, and later, the empty space where Kael's shoes used to be by the door. These visual fragments are frequently accompanied by "Auditory Recall"-the shrill, unceasing wail of sirens, or the flat, dispassionate tone of the police officer's voice delivering the news. When these memories surface, Leilani feels an intense "Overwhelm on Recall," a suffocating wave of grief, panic, and nausea that forces her to stop whatever she's doing, often finding herself gasping for air.

The profound impact of Kael's death has led Leilani to a deeply entrenched set of "Negative Appraisals." She constantly thinks, "My life has been destroyed by the trauma," convinced that any hope for a future she once envisioned is irrevocably lost. This conviction feeds a pervasive sense that "nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore," extending to her marriage, her friendships, and even her once-cherished career. She battles with profound existential questions, often concluding, "I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power," struggling to reconcile her suffering with any sense of order or justice in the world.

These overwhelming "Negative Appraisals" directly fuel Leilani's "Maladaptive Strategies." Because she believes her "life has been destroyed" and "nothing feels meaningful anymore," the thought of engaging with her forensic analyst duties, which demand meticulous attention and emotional detachment, feels impossible. She has begun to "Avoid Work or Study," calling in sick with increasing frequency or staring blankly at her computer screen when she does manage to log on, unable to focus on the intricate details of a case. The despair also makes her feel undeserving of care, leading to "Undereating"; she often skips meals entirely, her appetite completely gone. To escape the quiet of her home, where memories are most potent, she will "Delay Sleep," staying up until the early hours watching mindless television or scrolling on her phone, dreading the moment she has to close her eyes and confront the darkness.

Leilani's attempts at coping through these "Maladaptive Strategies" ironically exacerbate her memory difficulties. The chronic "Delay Sleep" leaves her physically exhausted but mentally agitated, making the "Auditory Recall" of sirens or the officer's voice more frequent and piercing in the quiet of the night. The "Snapshot Memories" of the accident return with greater intensity, often leading to even more severe "Overwhelm on Recall," sometimes leaving her physically trembling. Her efforts to suppress thoughts of Kael by staying constantly distracted often backfire, making the memories feel more intrusive and less controllable, springing forth unbidden at the slightest trigger.

This cycle is further reinforced as her "Maladaptive Strategies" feed back into her "Negative Appraisals." The disciplinary warnings she has received due to her "Avoidance of Work" only serve to confirm her belief that "her life has been destroyed" and that she is now utterly incapable. The physical toll of "Undereating" and the perpetual exhaustion from "Delaying Sleep" leave her feeling weak and perpetually drained, solidifying her conviction that "nothing in her life feels meaningful anymore" and that she is a broken version of her former self. Her deep conviction that "her life has been destroyed" and her "lost faith" makes the intrusive "Snapshot Memories" and "Auditory Recalls" feel even more crushing and inescapable. She interprets their return as proof that she will never recover, that the trauma is permanent, thus amplifying the "Overwhelm on Recall" and making her less likely to engage with the memories in a constructive way. She is certain that if she allows herself to fully remember, the pain will consume her entirely. Leilani came to therapy hoping for some relief, afraid that she might never escape the tightening grip of her grief and despair.
